learn: Lines can show movement. Curvy lines can show wind. Zigzag lines can show lightning.
Lines that lean can make things look like they are falling or running.
Artists choose lines to tell what is happening.
lessons.try: Draw a windy day using only lines.

learn: An outline is the line around the edge of a shape.
A contour line follows the edges slowly and carefully.
Try drawing your hand by slowly following its edge with your pencil.
check: The line around the edge of a shape
How should you draw a contour line?
lessons.try: Trace around your hand, then draw it again without tracing.

learn: You can draw a story in pictures, like a comic.
Each box shows one part: beginning, middle and end.
Lines show where characters move and how they feel.
check: How many parts did our comic have?
What do lines show in a comic?
A comic tells a story in...
lessons.try: Draw a three-box comic about a cat who finds a hat.

learn: Geometric shapes have neat, exact edges: circles, squares, triangles and rectangles.
Many buildings and machines use geometric shapes.
You can draw them with a ruler or by tracing objects.
check: Where do we often see geometric shapes?
What can help draw a neat circle?
lessons.try: Trace a cup to make circles and draw a picture with them.

learn: Organic shapes are free-form and curvy, like leaves, clouds and animals.
They are found in nature.
No two organic shapes are exactly alike.
check: Are organic shapes all the same?
lessons.try: Draw five different cloud shapes.

learn: Artists often mix both kinds of shapes in one picture.
A city skyline uses geometric buildings with organic trees and clouds.
The artist Henri Matisse cut paper into bright organic shapes to make art.
check: A city picture might have geometric buildings and organic...
Can one picture have both kinds of shapes?
lessons.try: Cut paper into geometric and organic shapes and arrange them into a picture.

learn: The primary colours are red, yellow and blue.
Mixing two primary colours makes a secondary colour: orange, green or purple.
Red and yellow make orange. Blue and yellow make green. Red and blue make purple.
lessons.try: Mix paints to make all three secondary colours.

learn: The colour wheel puts colours in a circle in rainbow order.
Primary colours are spaced apart, and secondary colours sit between them.
Rainbows go red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple.
check: What order does the colour wheel follow?
Which colour sits between red and yellow?
Which colour comes after green in a rainbow?
lessons.try: Paint your own six-colour wheel.

learn: Colours across from each other on the wheel are called complementary colours.
Red and green are opposites. Blue and orange are opposites. Yellow and purple are opposites.
Opposites side by side look bright and bold.
check: What is the opposite of red?
What is the opposite of blue?
Colours across from each other are...
lessons.try: Draw a red apple on a green background. Does it pop?

learn: Red, orange and yellow are warm colours.
They remind us of fire, the Sun and summer.
Warm colours can feel exciting and full of energy.
lessons.try: Paint a sunset using only warm colours.

learn: Blue, green and purple are cool colours.
They remind us of water, grass and the night sky.
Cool colours can feel calm and peaceful.
lessons.try: Paint an ocean using only cool colours.

learn: Artists choose colours to show feelings, or mood.
A stormy picture might use dark cool colours. A party picture might use bright warm colours.
The same scene can feel different in different colours.
check: Can the same scene feel different in different colours?
lessons.try: Draw the same tree twice: once in warm colours, once in cool. Compare.

units.t: Texture You Can See and Touch

learn: Real texture is how something actually feels: rough, smooth, bumpy, soft.
Sculptures and fabrics have real texture.
Collages can add real texture with sandpaper, cotton or yarn.
check: What can add real texture to a collage?
lessons.try: Make a texture collage with three things that feel different.

learn: Visual texture is texture you see in a drawing but cannot feel.
Artists draw lines, dots and patterns to make things look furry, scaly or bumpy.
The paper is still smooth, but the picture looks textured.
check: Texture you can see but not feel
How can you make a drawing look furry?
lessons.try: Draw a fish with scales using little curved lines.

learn: A rubbing copies real texture onto paper with a crayon.
You can stamp texture too, by pressing a sponge or a leaf in paint.
Combine rubbings to make a texture picture.
check: What tool do you use for a rubbing?
Can you cut rubbings into shapes?
lessons.try: Make rubbings of three surfaces and cut them into shapes for a picture.

learn: A pattern repeats colours, shapes or lines in order.
An AB pattern goes red, blue, red, blue. An ABC pattern goes red, blue, green, red, blue, green.
Patterns make art look organised and rhythmic.
check: What comes next: red, blue, green, red, blue, ...?
An AB pattern has how many parts that repeat?
lessons.try: Make an ABC pattern with stickers or stamps.

learn: People all over the world use patterns in their art.
Quilts, rugs, pottery and clothing often have patterns.
Patterns can be passed down in families and communities.
check: Do people around the world use patterns?
Can patterns be passed down in families?
lessons.try: Find a pattern on a piece of clothing or a blanket at home.

learn: A radial pattern grows out from the centre, like a flower or a snowflake.
Start with a shape in the middle and repeat shapes in rings around it.
Many windows and plates use radial patterns.
check: Where does a radial pattern start?
Which looks like a radial pattern?
How do you build a radial pattern?
lessons.try: Draw a radial flower starting from a dot in the middle.

learn: Things that are close to us look big. Things far away look small.
In a picture, draw a near tree big and a far tree small.
This helps a flat picture look deep.
check: A near tree should be drawn...
This helps a flat picture look...
lessons.try: Draw three trees: one near, one middle and one far.

learn: Things close to us are drawn lower on the page.
Things far away are drawn higher on the page, closer to the horizon.
The horizon line is where the land meets the sky.
check: Where do far things go on the page?
lessons.try: Draw a horizon line and place a house far away near it.

learn: When one thing is in front of another, it covers part of it. This is overlapping.
The thing in front looks closer.
Overlap hills, trees and houses to make a landscape.
check: One thing covering part of another
What could you overlap in a landscape?
lessons.try: Draw three hills that overlap.

learn: A print is made by pressing an inked surface onto paper.
You can make many copies of the same picture.
Fingerprints are tiny prints from your own fingers.
check: Pressing an inked surface onto paper
Can you make many copies of a print?
lessons.try: Make fingerprint animals with paint or an ink pad.

learn: Stamps can be made from potatoes cut by a grown-up, sponges or foam.
Dip the stamp in paint, press it down, lift it straight up.
Repeat stamps to make patterns.
check: How do you lift a stamp?
Who should cut a potato stamp?
lessons.try: Make a stamp pattern with a sponge.

learn: Draw into a foam tray with a pencil to make grooves.
Roll paint over it. The grooves stay white.
Press paper on top and peel it off to see your print. The picture is backwards.
check: What do pencil grooves become in the print?
What do you roll over the foam?
lessons.try: Make a foam print of your initial. Remember it will print backwards.

learn: A shape is flat. A form is 3D and has depth.
A circle is a shape. A ball (sphere) is a form.
A square is a shape. A box (cube) is a form.
check: A cube is the form of a...
lessons.try: Find three forms in your kitchen.

learn: Additive sculpture means adding pieces together, like building with clay.
Score (scratch) both pieces and add a little water to stick them together.
Smooth the joins with your fingers.
check: How do you stick clay pieces?
What do you do to the joins?
lessons.try: Make a clay animal by joining body, head and legs.

learn: Artists can make sculptures from things that would be thrown away.
Boxes, bottle caps, tubes and buttons can become robots, castles or animals.
Reusing materials helps the planet too.
check: What can found object sculptures be made from?
lessons.try: Build a sculpture from recycled boxes and tubes.

learn: Art shows how people live and what they value.
Long ago, people painted animals on cave walls in places like Lascaux, France.
Every culture has its own art.
check: What did ancient people paint on cave walls?
lessons.try: Look at a picture of cave paintings. What animals do you see?

learn: In Mexico, artists make colourful papel picado, paper cut into lacy patterns.
In Japan, artists fold paper into shapes. This is origami.
In Ghana, kente cloth is woven in bright patterns.
lessons.try: Fold a simple paper cup or boat (origami).

learn: Artists display their work so others can enjoy it.
Write your name and a title on your art.
When looking at friends' art, say one thing you like and why.
check: What do you write on your art?
What do you tell a friend about their art?
One thing you like and why
lessons.try: Choose two artworks and hold a mini art show at home.
